items.title: Lebesgue components of a positive finite measure are positive
items.statement: Let ν be a finite positive measure and μ a positive measure on the same measurable space. If ν=ν_ac+ν_s with ν_ac absolutely continuous with respect to μ and ν_s singular with respect to μ, then ν_ac and ν_s are positive measures.
items.strategy: Direct. Use a μ-null carrier for the singular component. On that carrier the absolutely continuous part vanishes; off it the singular part vanishes. The decomposition then identifies each component on each side as the restriction of the positive measure ν.

references.title: Richard F. Bass, Real Analysis for Graduate Students, Theorem 13.4 and §13.3, PDF pp. 100–104
John K. Hunter, Measure Theory, Theorem 6.27 and proof, §6.8 (notes pp. 75–77)

items.title: A sigma-finite positive measure has a nonnegative Radon–Nikodym density version
items.statement: Assume AC. If μ and ν are sigma-finite positive measures on the same measurable space and ν is absolutely continuous with respect to μ, then the Radon–Nikodym class dν/dμ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative μ-almost everywhere.
items.strategy: Direct. Build a common finite-measure exhaustion from sigma-finite covers. The Radon–Nikodym theorem supplies a real-valued representative with finite-piece integrability. On each finite piece, positivity of ν rules out a positive-measure set where the representative is bounded above by a negative constant; a countable union and a null-set version change finish.

references.title: Richard F. Bass, Real Analysis for Graduate Students, Theorem 13.4 and §13.3, PDF pp. 100–104
John K. Hunter, Measure Theory, Theorem 6.27 and proof, §6.8 (notes pp. 75–77)

items.title: Dominated statistical experiments
items.statement: A statistical experiment on (X,A) is dominated if one supplied sigma-finite positive measure μ on that same measurable space dominates every sampling law P_θ, meaning P_θ≪μ for every θ. The definition adds no parameter measurability.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.2 PDF pp. 30–33 and §3.2 PDF pp. 53–55
Joshua M. Tebbs, STAT 512 Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes, §9.3, PDF pp. 118–123
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §3, PDF pp. 3–5

items.title: Likelihood ratio as a Radon–Nikodym derivative
items.statement: For probability measures P₁ and P₀ on the same measurable space, take the unique Lebesgue decomposition P₁=P₁,ac+P₁,s relative to P₀ and define the likelihood-ratio density to be the P₀-almost-everywhere class dP₁,ac/dP₀. The components are positive, P₁,ac is finite, and a nonnegative measurable representative may be chosen under AC. This class is a full likelihood ratio for P₁ versus P₀ only when P₁≪P₀; otherwise the singular component is retained separately. No pointwise canonical function is specified.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.2 PDF pp. 30–33 and §3.2 PDF pp. 53–55
Joshua M. Tebbs, STAT 512 Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes, §9.3, PDF pp. 118–123

items.title: Likelihood densities
items.statement: Under AC and a dominated experiment with fixed sigma-finite positive measure μ, choose simultaneously for each θ a finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative p_θ of the Radon–Nikodym class dP_θ/dμ. For observed x the likelihood is L_x(θ)=p_θ(x), with no implied measurability in θ. Each p_θ is determined only μ-almost everywhere; no pointwise canonical version or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable Θ is implied. A likelihood is not a probability distribution on Θ.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.2 PDF pp. 30–33 and §3.2 PDF pp. 53–55
Joshua M. Tebbs, STAT 512 Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes, §9.3, PDF pp. 118–123
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §3, PDF pp. 3–5

items.title: Likelihood-ratio change of measure
items.statement: Assume AC and let P₀,P₁ be probability measures on one measurable space. Let r be a nonnegative representative of the likelihood-ratio class for P₁ versus P₀. If P₁≪P₀, then P₁=r dP₀ and E_{P₀}[g r]=E_{P₁}[g] for every nonnegative measurable g, and also for every real g integrable under P₁. Here E_{Pᵢ} means integration with respect to Pᵢ. Without P₁≪P₀, this identity need not hold because the singular component may be nonzero.
items.strategy: Direct. Uniqueness of Lebesgue decomposition identifies the absolutely continuous part with P₁ in the dominated case. The Radon–Nikodym representation gives a nonnegative density r and therefore the density measure r dP₀ equals P₁. Density integration proves the nonnegative identity; integrable real functions follow by applying it to positive and negative parts.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.2 PDF pp. 30–33 and §3.2 PDF pp. 53–55
Joshua M. Tebbs, STAT 512 Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes, §9.3, PDF pp. 118–123
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §3, PDF pp. 3–5

items.title: Equivalent dominating measures give equivalent likelihood ratios
items.statement: Assume AC. Let μ and ν be mutually absolutely continuous sigma-finite positive measures on one measurable space, and let (P_θ) be a statistical experiment dominated by both. Choose nonnegative density representatives p_θ^μ=dP_θ/dμ, p_θ^ν=dP_θ/dν, and h=dν/dμ. For each θ, p_θ^μ=h p_θ^ν μ-almost everywhere; h is positive μ-almost everywhere and depends only on the two dominators. Thus for each fixed pair θ,η, p_θ^μ/p_η^μ=p_θ^ν/p_η^ν μ-almost everywhere wherever the denominator is positive. No common exceptional null set for all pairs in an arbitrary uncountable Θ, no pointwise canonical versions, and no ratio value at a zero denominator are asserted.
items.strategy: Direct. Construct a common finite-measure exhaustion for the two sigma-finite dominators; the probability laws are finite on it, so the local Radon–Nikodym chain rule applies. The derivative h has a nonnegative version, and μ≪ν forces it to be positive μ-almost everywhere. Cancel the same positive data-only factor for each fixed pair, keeping its version-specific null sets.

references.title: Ryan Martin, Lecture Notes on Advanced Statistical Theory, §2.2 PDF pp. 30–33 and §3.2 PDF pp. 53–55
Joshua M. Tebbs, STAT 512 Mathematical Statistics Lecture Notes, §9.3, PDF pp. 118–123
Charles J. Geyer, Stat 5421 Lecture Notes: Exponential Families, §3, PDF pp. 3–5

items.title: A singular pair has no full likelihood ratio
items.statement: For P₀=δ₀ and P₁=δ₁ on {0,1}, the P₁-absolutely-continuous component relative to P₀ is zero and its P₀-a.e. likelihood-ratio class is zero, while the singular component is P₁. At x=1 the elementary quotient of counting-measure masses has denominator zero, and no function can represent all of P₁ as a density with respect to P₀.
items.strategy: Direct finite verification. Check the point-mass probability laws and counting-measure densities, identify the Lebesgue decomposition using the disjoint singleton carriers, and evaluate a proposed full density identity on {1}.

items.title: Bernoulli likelihood ratio and change of measure
items.statement: On X={0,1} with counting measure and parameter set Θ={0,1}, let P₀({1})=1/3, P₀({0})=2/3, P₁({1})=2/3, and P₁({0})=1/3. Both laws are dominated by counting measure. The likelihood ratio is r(0)=1/2 and r(1)=2, and for every real function g on this finite space, E_{P₀}[g r]=E_{P₁}[g].
items.strategy: Direct finite verification. Check the two-point measurable space and counting measure, verify that both laws are probability measures dominated by counting measure, compute the point-mass densities and their ratio, then expand both expectations for an arbitrary g.
